title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Morgan Lee
body:
Summary
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and standards across API design, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance objectives, and the ADR process. It is intended as the single source of truth for design decisions that affect product reliability, performance, security, and operational cost.

Scope
- Audience: engineers, tech leads, product managers, SRE, security reviewers.
- Applies to: hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployment flavors (control plane, serving runtime, pipelines, IaC).
- Excludes: marketing collateral and external customer-facing API docs (those live in the public docs portal).

Principles (applies across all sections)
1. Predictability: prefer designs with measurable SLOs and observable behavior.
2. Simplicity: default to simple, auditable implementations; optimize later for cost.
3. Backward compatibility: avoid breaking changes without an ADR and migration path.
4. Safety & least privilege: default secure configuration (RBAC, KMS for keys).
5. Ownership: every service/component has a named owner and runbook.

1) API Standards
- Versioning: use path-based semantic versioning: /api/v1/... for GA. Breaking changes require a major version bump and an ADR.
- OpenAPI: every public or internal API must have an OpenAPI 3.0 spec checked into api-definitions/ with CI validation (openapi-cli).
- Request/Response style: JSON over HTTPS; prefer RESTful resource endpoints for long-lived resources; use RPC-style endpoints only for complex actions with clear names.
- Idempotency: write operations must support idempotency via Idempotency-Key header where possible.
- Error model: standardized error envelope: {"code": "<short_code>", "message": "<human_message>", "retryable": "true|false"}. Map HTTP codes: 400 (client), 401/403 (auth), 404 (not_found), 429 (rate_limited), 500/503 (server).
- Rate limiting & throttling: default rate limits per tenant documented in pricing; 429 responses must include Retry-After header.
- Backwards compatibility policy: additive changes are allowed in minor versions; remove/rename fields only with major version and migration docs.
- API naming & endpoints example: /api/v1/generation, /api/v1/embeddings, /api/v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{version_id}/metrics.
- Security: OAuth2/Bearer tokens for inter-service and customer API auth; request must include x-request-id header.

2) Coding & Repo Standards
- Languages & frameworks: primary backend languages are Go (runtime & infra control plane) and Python (SDKs, evals). Use pre-commit hooks and linters (golangci-lint, black/isort/ruff).
- Style & patterns: follow language idioms. Avoid heavy framework magic in core runtime paths. Keep hot-path code review with at least two reviewers including a runtime owner for perf-sensitive changes.
- Tests: unit tests required; integration tests for any API contract change; performance/regression tests for runtime and model-serving changes. CI must run fast unit tests and gate slow integration tests on nightly/PR with labels.
- Branching & PRs: trunk-based development; PRs must include a descriptive changelog entry and target owner approval.
- Secrets: never check secrets into repo. Use Vault/KMS secrets in CI and runtime.

3) Infrastructure Standards
- IaC: Terraform modules under infra/modules/; pattern: module names prefixed rwd- (example: rwd-network, rwd-gpu-pool, rwd-k8s). All changes require plan output saved as an artifact in PR.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. Each environment has separate accounts/projects and limited blast radius.
- Network & security: default VPC with private subnets for compute; control plane endpoints are private for Dedicated/Private deployments. Use security groups and minimal ingress rules.
- Image & CI/CD: immutable container images built via the build pipeline; image tags use sha256 and semantic tags (example: rwd-runtime@sha256:<digest> and rwd-runtime:2026.01.15).
- Capacity naming & tagging: tags required: team, service, environment, cost-center, owner.

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Model packaging: models stored in model-registry with metadata: model_id, architecture, tokenizer_hash, quantization_profile, size, expected_max_seq. Use manifests in JSON stored alongside artifacts.
- Variant naming: <model>-<precision>-<variant> (e.g., oak-13b-4bit-quantized, pine-7b-fp16).
- Runtime constraints: per-model config must include min_gpu_type, max_batch_size, max_seq_len, kv_cache_support=true/false. These fields are strings in the manifest.
- Fallback & routing policy: define ordered fallback list in model catalog: primary -> cheaper-variant -> region-fallback. Automatic fallback must be configured per customer and respected by routing service.
- Warmup & KV cache: models that use KV cache must provide an optional warmup prompt set (up to 16 short prompts) to bootstrap cache after cold starts. Warmup steps are executed during instance lifecycle start.
- Quality gating: every model version must pass a smoke eval on a canonical prompt set before rollout (see applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks).

5) Observability Standards
- Core telemetry: every request must emit the following metrics with well-defined labels: requests_total, tokens_generated_total, latency_ms (histogram or summary), cache_hit_ratio, error_count_total. Labels: service, model_id, model_version, region, route, customer_tier.
- Logging: structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, request_id, model_id, model_version, user_id_hash, latency_ms, status, message. Log retention and forwarding rules in security-and-compliance/audit-logging.
- Tracing: distributed tracing enabled with OpenTelemetry. Sampling: default 10% sampling, 100% sampling on error and on traces flagged by canary experiments. Trace context must propagate x-request-id and traceparent.
- Dashboards & alerts: per-service dashboards (p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, error rate, token throughput). Alert ownership must be specified in alert metadata.
- On-call & runbooks: every alert has a runbook link and an owner team. Runbooks must include steps for triage, mitigation, and rollback.

Alerts reference table (canonical thresholds)
| Alert name | Trigger | Severity | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| High Error Rate | error_rate > 1% over 5m | SEV1 | eng-sre |
| Tail Latency Spike | p99 latency > 1000 ms for 10m | SEV2 | serving-runtime |
| Cache Eviction Surge | cache_hit_ratio < 30% for 5m | SEV2 | serving-runtime |
| Deployment Failure | rollout failure > 5% of canary | SEV1 | eng-platform |

6) Performance Standards & SLOs
- Default SLOs (hosted tier, generation requests <=512 tokens): p50 <= 200 ms, p95 <= 400 ms, p99 <= 800 ms. For dedicated customers SLOs are contract-specific and listed in the customer's SLA.
- Error budget: rolling 30-day error budget of 0.1% for SEV1-class errors on control plane operations; product-specific budgets defined in eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets.
- Benchmarking: all model onboarding includes a perf benchmark matrix: tokens/sec, latency at batch sizes [1,4,8], GPU utilization, memory footprint. Benchmarks are stored under eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
- Optimization guidance: use batching, KV caching, and quantization profiles as primary levers. Redwood Optimize team will publish suggested profiles per model (see quantization-profiles).

7) Decision Records (ADRs) Process
- When to write an ADR: any architecture decision that affects multiple teams, has long-lived operational implications, or changes SLOs must be captured.
- ADR template fields (flat list in a file): id, title, date, status (proposed/accepted/deprecated), context, decision, consequences, mitigations, owners, related_docs.
- ADR naming: ADR-YYYY-NNN short-title (example ADR-2026-001-model-routing).
- Approval flow: author -> owner_team review -> at least one cross-team approver (SRE or Security) -> published in architecture-and-standards and linked from related components.
- Review window: ADRs are published as draft for a 7 business day review before being accepted unless marked urgent (urgent requires explicit approval).

8) Rollout & Change Management
- Deployment strategy: default is canary followed by phased rollout (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%). Use feature flags to control rollout where possible.
- Rollout criteria: e2e smoke checks, canary metrics within expected thresholds (error rate, latency, token throughput). Rollback if any SEV1 is observed or if canary error rate increases >3x baseline for 10m.
- Post-release: 72-hour monitoring window with a post-deploy review and a short postmortem for any SEV2/SEV1 issues.

9) Ownership & Contacts
- Each major component must include owner, secondary owner, and on-call rotation in the repo README or component manifest. Examples: serving-runtime (owner: Maya Chen), routing-service (owner: Daniel Park), model-registry (owner: Priya Nair).

10) Appendices & Links

Change log

Notes and future work
- We will add concrete numeric guidance for large-sequence workloads and tighter SLOs for premium tiers.
- Add automation to validate OpenAPI specs and model manifests as part of PR checks.
